q: What is explicit cost?
r: A direct payment a firm makes to outsiders
Wages and rent are examples.
w: The value of the owner's own time
A cost the firm has already forgotten
Memory does not define a cost type.
A cost that never involves money

q: What is implicit cost?
r: The opportunity cost of resources the firm already owns
The owner's lost salary is an example.
w: A direct cash payment to suppliers
A cost listed on the income statement
A cost that varies with output

q: How is economic profit calculated?
r: Total revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
It counts opportunity costs as well as cash costs.
w: Total revenue minus explicit costs only
That is not a profit measure.

q: A shop earns $90,000, pays $60,000 in cash costs and the owner gave up a $40,000 job. What is the economic profit?
What does a shutdown decision compare in the short run?
r: Revenue against variable costs
If revenue cannot cover them, producing loses more.
w: Fixed costs are owed either way.

q: In the short run, when should a firm shut down?
r: When price is below average variable cost
It would lose more by producing than by closing.
w: When price is below average total cost
It may still cover variable costs.
When profit is slightly lower than last year
That alone is not a shutdown signal.

q: What is total fixed cost for a firm with $3,000 rent and $1,000 insurance?
r: Both costs stay the same at every output level.

q: Total cost is $10,000 for 500 units. What is average total cost?
r: $20 per unit
$10,000 divided by 500 equals $20.
w: That is the number of units.

q: Total cost rises from $10,000 to $10,150 when output rises by 10 units. What is marginal cost?
r: $15 per unit
$150 divided by 10 equals $15.

q: Why does the marginal cost curve eventually rise?
r: Diminishing returns make each extra unit cost more
Added workers become less productive.
w: Fixed costs rise with each unit
Fixed costs do not change with output.
This is not an economic cause.

q: What is a perfectly competitive firm's marginal revenue equal to?
r: The market price
It can sell every unit at the same price.

q: A perfectly competitive firm should produce where:
r: Marginal cost equals price
That maximizes profit when price equals marginal revenue.

q: What happens to a monopolist's price compared with a competitive firm's price?
r: A monopolist usually charges more and produces less
It has market power and restricts output.
w: A monopolist charges less and produces more
A monopolist must charge the market price
A monopolist produces at zero profit

q: What is a barrier to entry?
r: Something that makes it hard for new firms to join a market
Patents and high start-up costs are examples.
w: A rule that lets any firm join freely
A fee customers pay at a store

q: What is a natural monopoly?
r: A market best served by one firm because of very high fixed costs
Utilities like water often fit this pattern.
w: A monopoly created by hiding resources
A market with many equal sellers
A monopoly that exists only in nature reserves

q: What is price discrimination?
r: Charging different customers different prices for the same good
Student discounts are an example.
w: Refusing to sell to certain groups
Charging every customer the same price

q: A cinema sells cheaper tickets to seniors. Which condition must hold for this to raise profit?
r: Groups have different sensitivity to price and can be kept apart
Sellers charge more to the less sensitive group.
w: Identical buyers leave no room to discriminate.
Resale between groups must be easy
Easy resale would erase the price gap.
The seller must have no market power
It needs some power to set prices.

q: What is a loss leader?
r: A product sold at a loss to draw customers in
Stores hope buyers add other, profitable items.
w: The manager responsible for a loss
That is not the retail term.
A product that is always unprofitable
The loss is intentional and temporary.
A product given away for free forever
That is a giveaway, not a loss leader.

q: What does cost-plus pricing do?
r: Adds a markup to the cost of a product
It makes sure each sale covers costs and some profit.
w: Sets the price at what rivals charge
Sets prices by what buyers will pay
Sets prices to the lowest possible level

q: A product costs $24 to make and the firm adds a 25% markup on cost. What is the price?
r: $24 plus $6 equals $30.

q: What is profit margin?
r: Profit as a percent of revenue
It shows how much of each sales dollar is kept.
w: Revenue as a percent of costs
Costs as a percent of assets
Assets as a percent of equity

q: A firm earns $15,000 profit on $200,000 revenue. What is its profit margin?
r: $15,000 divided by $200,000 equals 0.075.
w: That is the dollar amount in thousands.

q: What is a firm's break-even quantity?
r: The output where total revenue equals total cost
Profit is zero there.
w: The output that earns the largest profit
The output where costs are zero
The output where revenue is zero

q: Fixed costs are $9,000. Each unit sells for $15 and costs $6 to make. What is the break-even quantity?
r: 1,000 units
$9,000 divided by a $9 margin equals 1,000.
w: That is the fixed cost in dollars.

q: If a firm sells above its break-even quantity, what happens?
r: It earns a profit
Revenue exceeds total cost beyond that point.

q: Which is an example of a variable cost for a bakery?
r: Flour used for each loaf
It rises and falls with the number of loaves.

q: Why do firms often use economies of scope?
r: Producing related goods together lowers average cost
They share equipment and expertise.
w: Producing only one good raises cost
That is not what scope means.
Producing unrelated goods in different countries

q: A bakery that also sells coffee uses the same staff and counters for both. Which concept explains the lower cost?
r: Economies of scope
Sharing resources across related products cuts cost.

q: What is the long run in economics?
r: A period long enough for all inputs to be varied
Firms can change plant size and enter or exit.
w: A period longer than ten years exactly
The length is not fixed by years.
A period when prices never change
A period when firms cannot produce

q: What is the short run in economics?
r: A period when at least one input is fixed
Plant size cannot change quickly.
w: A period when every input can be changed
A period lasting exactly one month

q: What happens in a competitive industry when firms earn economic profit?
r: New firms enter and profit shrinks
Entry raises supply and lowers prices.

q: What happens in a competitive industry when firms suffer losses?
r: Some firms exit and prices rise
Less supply lifts price back toward cost.

q: What is the accounting equation for profit?
r: Profit equals revenue minus expenses
It is the bottom-line measure.
w: Profit equals price divided by quantity

q: Which is a typical overhead cost for a retail store?
r: Utilities and rent
They are not tied to a single product.
w: The cost of each item sold
That is cost of goods sold.

q: Total revenue is $500,000, cost of goods sold is $300,000 and operating expenses are $120,000. What is operating profit?
What does a business do with the resources it takes in?
r: Turns them into goods or services that customers value
Production creates value.
w: Stores them without ever using them
Burns them to heat the factory

q: What is a limited partnership?
r: A partnership where some partners have limited liability
At least one general partner has unlimited liability.
w: A partnership where no one is liable for debts
A partnership limited to two people
A partnership with no profit sharing

q: What is a general partnership?
r: A partnership where all partners share management and liability
Each partner can be responsible for business debts.
w: A partnership where only one partner is liable
A partnership run by the government

q: What is a partnership agreement?
r: A contract stating each partner's duties, shares and rights
It helps avoid disputes.
w: A tax form filed with the state
A loan from a bank to a partner

q: What is a disadvantage of a partnership?
r: Partners can disagree and may be liable for each other's acts
Shared control brings shared risk.
w: It must be run by a single person
It pays no taxes at all
Partners pay tax on their share.

q: What is double taxation?
r: Corporate profit taxed at the firm and again as dividends
Owners pay tax on the same income twice.
w: Paying sales tax at two stores
Filing two tax returns in one year
Paying tax twice on a purchase
That is not the usual meaning.

q: What is an S corporation?
r: A corporation taxed through its owners' returns
It avoids double taxation under certain rules.
w: A corporation owned by the state
A corporation that never pays tax
It is a U.S. tax status.

q: What is a board of directors?
r: Elected leaders who oversee a corporation's management
They represent shareholders.
w: A bank that lends to the company

q: What is a shareholder?
r: An owner of shares in a corporation
Shareholders may vote and receive dividends.
w: A lender who holds the company's loans
A worker paid by the hour

q: What is a stakeholder?
r: Anyone affected by a business's decisions
Customers, workers and neighbors are examples.
w: Only the owners of the business
Only the managers of the business
Only the competitors of the business

q: What is vertical integration?
r: A firm owning several stages of its supply chain
A maker might buy its supplier.
w: Two rivals merging at the same stage
A firm selling to many countries
A firm splitting into smaller units

q: What is horizontal integration?
r: Merging with a competitor at the same stage of production
It can raise market share.
w: Buying a supplier of raw materials
Opening a store in a new country

q: What is a merger?
r: Two companies combining into one
They share assets, staff and debts.

q: What is an acquisition?
r: One company buying control of another
The target may keep operating as a unit.
w: Two firms agreeing to share a logo
A firm hiring a new CEO

q: What is a hostile takeover?
r: An acquisition the target company's management opposes
The buyer goes directly to shareholders.
w: An acquisition that both sides welcome

q: What is a business plan's executive summary?
r: A short overview of the whole plan
It is written to grab a reader's interest.
w: A list of every employee's pay
A full set of financial statements
Those come later in the plan.

q: What is a franchisee?
r: A person who buys the right to run a business under a brand
They pay fees and follow the franchisor's system.
w: The company that owns the brand
A supplier of the brand's goods

q: What is a franchisor?
r: The company that licenses its brand and system to others
It earns fees and royalties.
w: The person who runs the local outlet
The customer who buys the product
The bank that lends to the outlet

q: What is a royalty?
r: A payment for the ongoing use of a brand or idea
Franchisees pay royalties to the franchisor.
w: A fine for breaking a rule

q: What is entrepreneurship's role in an economy?
r: Creating new businesses, jobs and ideas
Start-ups drive innovation.
